thinkers.name: John Locke
thinkers.line: English philosopher whose Two Treatises of Government (1689) grounded government in natural rights and consent; a founding text of liberalism.

thinkers.name: Adam Smith
thinkers.line: Scottish economist and moral philosopher; The Wealth of Nations (1776) is often called the first comprehensive defense of free markets.

thinkers.name: Thomas Paine
thinkers.line: Pamphleteer whose Common Sense (January 1776) made the popular case for American independence.

thinkers.name: Thomas Jefferson
thinkers.line: Drafted the Declaration of Independence in 1776; his ideas on limited government shaped American political thought.

thinkers.name: Frédéric Bastiat
thinkers.line: French economist and legislator; The Law (1850) argues law should protect persons and property and warns against 'legal plunder.'

thinkers.name: John Stuart Mill
thinkers.line: English philosopher; On Liberty (1859) defends individual freedom on utilitarian grounds.

thinkers.name: Lysander Spooner
thinkers.line: Abolitionist and individualist anarchist; challenged the postal monopoly in 1844 and wrote No Treason: The Constitution of No Authority (1870).

thinkers.name: Henry David Thoreau
thinkers.line: Jailed in 1846 for refusing his poll tax over slavery and the Mexican War; his 1849 essay became known as 'Civil Disobedience.'

thinkers.name: Benjamin R. Tucker
thinkers.line: Leading American individualist anarchist; edited the journal Liberty from 1881 to 1908.

thinkers.name: Ludwig von Mises
thinkers.line: Austrian School economist; author of Socialism (1922) and Human Action (1949); the Mises Institute is named for him.

thinkers.name: Henry Hazlitt
thinkers.line: Journalist and economist; wrote Economics in One Lesson (1946) and helped found the Foundation for Economic Education.

thinkers.name: Leonard E. Read
thinkers.line: Founded the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946 and led it until his death.

thinkers.name: F. A. Hayek
thinkers.line: Austrian-British economist; wrote The Road to Serfdom (1944), founded the Mont Pelerin Society (1947) and shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in economics.

thinkers.name: Ayn Rand
thinkers.line: Novelist and philosopher who developed Objectivism; Atlas Shrugged (1957) drew many readers to individualism.

thinkers.name: Milton Friedman
thinkers.line: Chicago economist; Capitalism and Freedom (1962), the 1976 Nobel Prize, and Free to Choose (1980); proposed school vouchers and argued for a volunteer military.

thinkers.name: Karl Hess
thinkers.line: Former Goldwater speechwriter who moved toward anarchism; his essay 'The Death of Politics' (1969) became a rallying point for libertarians.

thinkers.name: Tonie Nathan
thinkers.line: 1972 Libertarian vice-presidential nominee and the first woman to receive an electoral vote.

thinkers.name: Murray Rothbard
thinkers.line: Economist and leading theorist of anarcho-capitalism; wrote For a New Liberty (1973), helped found Cato, and later argued for a 'paleo' populist strategy.

thinkers.name: Ed Clark
thinkers.line: 1980 Libertarian presidential nominee whose 921,128 votes stood as the party's record for more than three decades.

thinkers.name: Robert Nozick
thinkers.line: Philosopher whose Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) defended a minimal state and won the 1975 National Book Award.

thinkers.name: David Nolan
thinkers.line: Co-founder and first national chair of the Libertarian Party; created the Nolan Chart (1971).

institutions.name: Libertarian Party
institutions.line: U.S. political party founded December 11, 1971; it has run a presidential candidate in every election since 1972.

institutions.name: Mises Caucus
institutions.line: Faction within the Libertarian Party founded in 2017 by Michael Heise; won control of the national committee at the 2022 convention.

institutions.name: Reason
institutions.line: Libertarian magazine and website ('Free Minds and Free Markets') founded in 1968, with a video arm, Reason TV.

institutions.name: Reason Foundation
institutions.line: Policy research nonprofit founded in 1978 that publishes Reason.

institutions.name: Cato Institute
institutions.line: Washington, D.C., public-policy research organization founded in 1977 by Ed Crane with Charles Koch and Murray Rothbard; mission centers on individual liberty, limited government, free markets and peace.

institutions.name: Mises Institute
institutions.line: Educational, research and publishing institute for Austrian economics, founded in 1982 by Lew Rockwell in Auburn, Alabama.

institutions.name: Foundation for Economic Education (FEE)
institutions.line: Founded in 1946 by Leonard Read with Henry Hazlitt; often called the oldest free-market think tank in the U.S.; now based in Atlanta.

institutions.name: Institute for Justice
institutions.line: Libertarian public-interest law firm founded in 1991 by Chip Mellor and Clint Bolick; litigates economic liberty, property rights, school choice and free speech cases.

institutions.name: Pacific Legal Foundation
institutions.line: Public-interest law firm founded in Sacramento in 1973, described as the oldest libertarian public-interest law firm; focuses on property rights, equality and opportunity, and separation of powers.

institutions.name: Goldwater Institute
institutions.line: Phoenix think tank founded in 1988 with Sen. Barry Goldwater's support; added a constitutional litigation arm in 2007.

institutions.name: Students For Liberty
institutions.line: Student organization formed in 2008 after a conference at Columbia University; supports libertarian student groups.

institutions.name: Young Americans for Liberty
institutions.line: Campus organization founded in 2008 out of the Students for Ron Paul effort.

institutions.name: Institute for Humane Studies
institutions.line: Founded in 1961 by economist F. A. 'Baldy' Harper to support classical liberal scholarship; associated with George Mason University since 1985.

institutions.name: Atlas Network
institutions.line: Founded in 1981 by Antony Fisher; links several hundred free-market think tanks in more than 100 countries.

institutions.name: Mont Pelerin Society
institutions.line: International society of classical liberal scholars founded by Hayek in 1947 near Lake Geneva.

institutions.name: Libertarianism.org
institutions.line: Online library with an encyclopedia of libertarian thinkers and ideas, essays and podcasts.

institutions.name: Free State Project
institutions.line: Effort launched in 2001 to move 20,000 liberty-minded people to New Hampshire (chosen in 2003); it passed 20,000 pledges in 2016.

institutions.name: Advocates for Self-Government
institutions.line: Distributes the 'World's Smallest Political Quiz,' a version of the Nolan Chart.

officeholders.name: Rand Paul
officeholders.line: Describes himself as a constitutional conservative and has called himself libertarian-leaning; son of Ron Paul.

officeholders.name: Thomas Massie
officeholders.line: Described by Reason and others as a libertarian Republican; lost his May 19, 2026 primary to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein, so his term ends in January 2027.

officeholders.name: Mike Lee
officeholders.line: Described by the Associated Press as a libertarian-leaning conservative.

officeholders.name: Jared Polis
officeholders.line: Was the only Democratic member of the House Liberty Caucus; Reason has called him perhaps the most libertarian governor in America, a label other libertarians dispute.

officeholders.name: Justin Amash
officeholders.line: Describes himself as a libertarian; joined the LP in April 2020 as the first Libertarian in Congress, ran in the 2024 Republican U.S. Senate primary, and returned to the LP in 2025.

officeholders.name: Javier Milei
officeholders.line: Economist widely described as a libertarian; won the November 2023 runoff with 55.7%.

officeholders.name: Ron Paul
officeholders.line: Libertarian presidential nominee in 1988 and Republican presidential candidate in 2008 and 2012.

officeholders.name: Gary Johnson
officeholders.line: Libertarian presidential nominee in 2012 and 2016; won 3.28% in 2016, the party's best result.

officeholders.name: Marshall Burt
officeholders.office: Former Wyoming state representative, House District 39 (elected 2020)
officeholders.line: Won his seat in 2020 as a Libertarian, the party's first state legislative win in about two decades; lost re-election in 2022.

media.name: Reason TV
media.line: Reason's video arm, publishing documentaries and commentary, also on YouTube.

media.name: EconTalk
media.line: Weekly economics interview podcast hosted by Russ Roberts since 2006, from Liberty Fund's Library of Economics and Liberty.

media.name: Free to Choose
media.line: Milton and Rose Friedman's 1980 PBS series and companion best-seller on markets and freedom.

media.name: Stossel TV
media.line: Online channel journalist John Stossel launched in 2019 after careers at ABC News and Fox Business.

media.name: Part of the Problem
media.line: Libertarian podcast hosted by comedian Dave Smith, a member of the LP's Mises Caucus.

media.name: Free Thoughts
media.line: Libertarianism.org's podcast on libertarian ideas and history.

media.name: The Road to Serfdom (F. A. Hayek, 1944)
media.line: Hayek's warning against central economic planning; a Reader's Digest condensation reached a mass audience in 1945.

media.name: Economics in One Lesson (Henry Hazlitt, 1946)
media.line: Widely read short primer on free-market economics.

media.name: Capitalism and Freedom (Milton Friedman, 1962)
media.line: Case for free trade, school vouchers and limited government from a Nobel economist.

media.name: For a New Liberty (Murray Rothbard, 1973)
media.line: Often called the first modern free-market anarchist manifesto; free from the Mises Institute.

media.name: The Machinery of Freedom (David Friedman, 1973)
media.line: Consequentialist case that law and defense could be supplied privately.

media.name: Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Robert Nozick, 1974)
media.line: Philosophical defense of the minimal state; won the National Book Award.
